lessonTitle: Type A and Type B Adverse Drug Reactions, Organ Toxicity and Teratogenicity

blocks.text: In the late 1950s, babies were born with severely shortened limbs after their mothers took a sedative for morning sickness. The drug had passed animal tests that no one had designed to look for this harm. The disaster reshaped how drugs are tested, licensed and monitored, and it is why we classify adverse reactions by how they arise.

blocks.markdown: An **adverse drug reaction (ADR)** is a harmful, unintended response to a drug at doses normally used in humans. ADRs are classified by mechanism so that clinicians can predict, prevent and manage them. The commonest classification separates **Type A (augmented)** from **Type B (bizarre)** reactions.

blocks.title: Type A and Type B reactions
blocks.text: Type A (augmented) reactions are exaggerations of the known pharmacological effect: dose-dependent, predictable, common, with low mortality. Type B (bizarre) reactions are unrelated to the drug's known pharmacology: not dose-dependent in the usual sense, unpredictable, uncommon, and with a higher mortality. Many Type B reactions are immunological (allergic) or idiosyncratic, often with a genetic susceptibility.

blocks.caption: Type A versus Type B adverse reactions.
rows: Stop the drug and avoid it in future
Hypoglycaemia with insulin; bleeding with warfarin; bradycardia with a beta-blocker; drowsiness with an antihistamine
Anaphylaxis with penicillin; Stevens-Johnson syndrome with carbamazepine or allopurinol; malignant hyperthermia with volatile anaesthetics

blocks.title: Classifying a reaction
blocks.prompt: Classify each reaction as Type A or Type B and justify: (1) a patient on ramipril develops dizziness and a fall in blood pressure after the dose is doubled; (2) another patient develops an urticarial rash and wheeze within an hour of the first dose of amoxicillin.

steps.text: Ask: is the harm an exaggeration of the drug's known pharmacology? Ramipril lowers blood pressure; excessive lowering is simply more of the intended effect.
Ask: is it dose-related and predictable? The hypotension followed a dose increase, so it is dose-dependent. Case 1 is Type A.

For case 2, amoxicillin has no pharmacological action that produces urticaria and bronchospasm. This is an immune-mediated hypersensitivity (IgE) reaction, unrelated to dose and unpredictable in a given patient. Case 2 is Type B.
Consequences differ: reduce the ramipril dose in case 1; stop amoxicillin and record penicillin allergy in case 2.

blocks.answer: Case 1 is Type A (augmented); case 2 is Type B (bizarre, immunological).

blocks.markdown: **Organ toxicity.** The liver and kidneys are exposed to high drug concentrations and are major sites of metabolism and excretion, so they are frequently injured. **Hepatotoxicity** may be dose-dependent and predictable (paracetamol overdose, where a toxic metabolite, NAPQI, overwhelms glutathione) or idiosyncratic (isoniazid hepatitis; flucloxacillin cholestatic jaundice; co-amoxiclav). Patterns include hepatocellular, cholestatic or mixed injury. **Nephrotoxicity** arises through reduced renal perfusion (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors in volume depletion), direct tubular injury (aminoglycosides, vancomycin, contrast media), or interstitial nephritis (penicillins, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors).

items: Hepatotoxic drugs: paracetamol (overdose), isoniazid, flucloxacillin, methotrexate, amiodarone, valproate.
Nephrotoxic drugs: aminoglycosides (gentamicin), NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and ARBs (with volume depletion), contrast media, lithium (long term).
Risk rises with pre-existing organ disease, older age, dehydration and combination of several toxic drugs.
Monitoring: liver function tests, urea and electrolytes, creatinine, and drug levels for narrow-index drugs.

blocks.title: Monitor the vulnerable organ
blocks.text: Know the organ a drug can injure and monitor it: creatinine and drug levels for gentamicin, liver tests for methotrexate and isoniazid. Early detection of a rising creatinine or ALT usually allows the drug to be stopped before irreversible damage.

blocks.markdown: **Teratogenicity.** A teratogen is a substance that causes structural malformation of the fetus. Risk depends on dose, gestational timing (organogenesis in the first trimester is the most sensitive for structural defects; later exposure affects growth or function) and genetic susceptibility. Established teratogens include thalidomide (limb defects), valproate (neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental effects), isotretinoin and other retinoids, warfarin (first trimester embryopathy), methotrexate, mycophenolate, and ACE inhibitors and ARBs (fetal renal toxicity in later pregnancy).

**How teratogens are identified.** Pre-marketing animal reproductive studies give a first signal but cannot be trusted alone because species differ (thalidomide was not clearly teratogenic in standard rodent tests). Human evidence comes from case reports, spontaneous reporting, pregnancy registries and cohort or case-control studies. Randomised trials in pregnancy are generally unethical, so for most drugs data is limited and caution is needed. **Avoidance** includes pre-conception counselling, effective contraception for women of childbearing potential taking known teratogens, pregnancy testing, folic acid supplementation where indicated, using safer alternatives, and stopping or switching the drug before conception where possible.

blocks.title: Do not stop treatment without advice
blocks.text: Pregnant women with epilepsy or other serious illness should not stop essential treatment suddenly. Uncontrolled disease can harm mother and fetus; the aim is specialist planning, preferably before conception, to choose the safest effective regimen at the lowest effective dose.

blocks.title: Assessing a drug in early pregnancy
blocks.prompt: A woman at 6 weeks of pregnancy has been taking lisinopril for hypertension. Outline the reasoning for the prescriber.

steps.text: Identify the drug class: ACE inhibitors are linked to fetal renal toxicity, oligohydramnios and skull ossification defects, mainly with exposure in the second and third trimesters, and are avoided in pregnancy.
Consider timing: at 6 weeks the embryo is in organogenesis, and exposure should be stopped promptly rather than continued until the next routine review.
Choose an alternative with better pregnancy safety data, for example labetalol or nifedipine, and arrange follow-up of blood pressure.
Document the exposure, counsel the patient about the risk and report it to pregnancy surveillance systems where appropriate.

blocks.answer: Stop the ACE inhibitor, switch to a safer antihypertensive such as labetalol or nifedipine, counsel and monitor.

blocks.title: Use the questions
blocks.text: To classify: is it dose-related and a known pharmacological extension (Type A) or not (Type B)? To assess pregnancy risk: what is the drug, when in gestation and what is the alternative?

points: Type A reactions are predictable, dose-related exaggerations of drug action; Type B reactions are unpredictable, often immunological, and need the drug stopped.
Liver and kidney are common targets of drug toxicity through direct injury, toxic metabolites, haemodynamic effects or immune mechanisms; monitor the vulnerable organ.
Teratogens are identified through human surveillance as well as animal studies, and risk is reduced by planning, contraception and choosing safer alternatives.

questions.stem: Which feature best characterises a Type A (augmented) adverse drug reaction?

options.text: It is dose-related and an exaggeration of the drug's known pharmacology
It is unpredictable and unrelated to the drug's action
It occurs only after years of treatment

questions.correctOptionText: It is dose-related and an exaggeration of the drug's known pharmacology

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Type A reactions are predictable extensions of the drug's pharmacology.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: timing is not what defines Type A.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: immunological mechanisms characterise many Type B reactions.

questions.explanation: Type A reactions arise from the drug's expected pharmacological effect being too great, and so they are dose-dependent and common. Management is usually to reduce the dose or change the regimen.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man develops a widespread blistering rash with mucosal involvement two weeks after starting allopurinol. How should this reaction be classified and managed?

options.text: Type B reaction; stop the drug and avoid it in future
Type A reaction; halve the dose
Type A reaction; continue with close observation
Type B reaction; reduce the dose and rechallenge at once

questions.correctOptionText: Type B reaction; stop the drug and avoid it in future

distractorRationale.a: Correct: severe cutaneous reactions are idiosyncratic or immune mediated and need permanent withdrawal.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: the reaction is not an extension of allopurinol's pharmacology.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: continuing risks a life-threatening reaction.

questions.explanation: Stevens-Johnson-type reactions are unpredictable and not related to the drug's known action, so they are Type B. The drug must be stopped immediately and recorded as an allergy or intolerance to prevent re-exposure.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with a chest infection is dehydrated and is given gentamicin and also takes ibuprofen. Her creatinine rises over three days. What is the most likely mechanism of kidney injury?

options.text: Direct tubular toxicity from gentamicin plus reduced renal perfusion from the NSAID

questions.correctOptionText: Direct tubular toxicity from gentamicin plus reduced renal perfusion from the NSAID

distractorRationale.a: Correct: aminoglycosides injure proximal tubular cells and NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-dependent renal blood flow, especially with dehydration.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: first-pass metabolism is not a mechanism of kidney injury.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: bile duct obstruction does not explain a rising creatinine here.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: NSAIDs reduce, not increase, renal perfusion in volume depletion.

questions.explanation: Gentamicin accumulates in proximal tubular cells and damages them, while NSAIDs block vasodilatory prostaglandins, lowering glomerular perfusion. Dehydration and older age amplify both effects, so levels and renal function must be monitored.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a well-established human teratogen requiring effective contraception during use in women of childbearing potential?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: retinoids cause craniofacial, cardiac and CNS malformations.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: paracetamol is generally regarded as acceptable in pregnancy at standard doses.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: folic acid reduces neural tube defect risk.

questions.explanation: Isotretinoin is a vitamin A derivative with a high risk of major malformations, so its use in women of childbearing potential requires pregnancy prevention programmes. Folic acid and standard-dose paracetamol are not teratogenic.

questions.stem: Why are animal reproductive studies alone insufficient to exclude teratogenicity in humans?

options.text: Species differ in metabolism and susceptibility, so a drug safe in animals may still harm human embryos
Animals cannot become pregnant under laboratory conditions
Teratogenicity is purely a Type A reaction

questions.correctOptionText: Species differ in metabolism and susceptibility, so a drug safe in animals may still harm human embryos

distractorRationale.a: Correct: species variation means animal findings neither prove nor exclude human risk.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: animal pregnancy studies are routine.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: teratogenicity is a separate category and not a Type A reaction.

questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetics and embryonic sensitivity differ between species, as the thalidomide experience showed. Human surveillance (case reports, registries, observational studies) is therefore essential.

questions.stem: True or false: Type B adverse reactions are generally predictable from the known pharmacology of the drug.
questions.explanation: Type B reactions are bizarre: they are unrelated to the drug's known pharmacology and so cannot be predicted from it. They often involve immune or genetic mechanisms.

questions.stem: Contrast Type A and Type B adverse drug reactions with two examples of each, and state how the management differs.
markingGuide: Type A: augmented, predictable extension of pharmacology, dose-related, common, low mortality
Type A examples: bleeding with warfarin, hypoglycaemia with insulin or sulfonylurea, bradycardia with beta-blocker
Type B: bizarre, unrelated to known pharmacology, unpredictable, uncommon, higher mortality, often immune or idiosyncratic
Type B examples: penicillin anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome with allopurinol or carbamazepine
Management: Type A reduce dose or adjust; Type B stop the drug and record the reaction to avoid re-exposure
questions.explanation: The key distinction is whether the reaction is a predictable extension of the drug's action. That determines whether dose adjustment can be sufficient or whether permanent avoidance is necessary.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with a body mass index of 19 presents 24 hours after taking an unknown quantity of paracetamol tablets. Explain the mechanism of paracetamol hepatotoxicity and why it is classed as a dose-dependent reaction.
markingGuide: At therapeutic doses paracetamol is mainly conjugated (glucuronidation and sulfation) and a small fraction is oxidised by CYP enzymes to NAPQI
In overdose the conjugation pathways saturate and more NAPQI forms; glutathione is depleted
Unneutralised NAPQI binds to hepatocyte proteins causing centrilobular necrosis
The harm increases with dose and is predictable, so it is a Type A (augmented, dose-dependent) reaction
Risk factors: malnutrition, chronic alcohol use, enzyme inducers; treatment is N-acetylcysteine, which replenishes glutathione, with early presentation giving better outcomes
questions.explanation: Toxicity results from saturation of safe metabolic pathways and depletion of the protective glutathione pool, so damage is proportional to dose. That dose-dependence is why it is a Type A reaction despite being severe.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy who is planning pregnancy takes sodium valproate. Explain how drugs are identified as teratogenic and outline how the risk should be managed.
markingGuide: Identification: animal reproductive studies give an initial signal but are limited by species differences
Human data: case reports, spontaneous reporting, pregnancy registries, cohort and case-control studies; RCTs generally unethical
Valproate is a known teratogen: neural tube defects, other malformations and neurodevelopmental effects
Management: pre-conception review by a specialist, switching to a safer alternative where possible, using the lowest effective dose
Effective contraception while on teratogenic therapy, folic acid supplementation, and informed discussion of risks and benefits
Do not stop the antiepileptic abruptly without advice because seizures also endanger mother and fetus
questions.explanation: Teratogen identification relies on human surveillance, and management centres on planned pre-conception change to the safest effective regimen. Abrupt withdrawal is dangerous because uncontrolled seizures carry their own risks.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man treated for tuberculosis develops nausea, dark urine and jaundice. His ALT is 12 times the upper limit of normal. Which drug is the most likely cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: isoniazid, along with rifampicin and pyrazinamide, is a recognised cause of hepatocellular injury.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: unlikely cause of hepatitis of this pattern.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: not hepatotoxic at standard doses.

questions.explanation: A marked rise in ALT with jaundice in a patient on antituberculous therapy suggests drug-induced hepatocellular injury. Isoniazid is a classical cause, so liver function is monitored and the drugs are stopped or modified under specialist advice.
